newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa first oil seen sold at premium to Brent.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa first oil seen sold at premium to Brent.

text.p: South Africa plans to sell crude from its first offshore oilfield at a premium to international benchmark North Sea Brent Blend, Central Energy Fund deputy general manager Brian Casey said on Wednesday.

"Everybody appears to be happy at this stage that, prior to the large physical trials that they will do, the crude oil will attract a premium to Brent," he told Reuters after a briefing by CEF to the parliamentary minerals and energy committee.
The first shipment of 600,000 barrels of oil from the Oribi oilfield 140 km from Mosselbay is due to arrive in Cape Town next week and is destined for the Caltex refinery in South Africa.
Caltex is a joint venture between Texaco Inc and Chevron Corp.
The second shipment has been sold to Total, which operates the Natref refinery with Sasol.
Casey said that initial tests had shown that the Oribi crude oil is of very high quality.

"It is a 42-43 API and has a sulphur content of about 0.15, which means that it is very similar to the Nigerian Brass River crude which trades usually at a premium to Brent North Sea oil," Casey said.
API is a universally accepted scale adopted by the American Petroleum Institute to measure the quality of oil. The higher the API, the lighter the crude.
"So Oribi crude will be selling on the market at a Brent-related number plus premium," Casey said.
CEF manages the government's Strategic Fuel Fund (SFF), which was set up under apartheid to ensure that South Africa had enough oil despite sanctions against it by most oil majors.

CEF acting general manager Howard Roberts told the committee that this function had ended with the lifting of sanctions in 1992 and SFF now only managed the country's strategic oil stocks of about 39 million barrels by buying and selling oil.
"Commercial trading is done on a no risk policy," he said.
Casey said that SFF had a mixture of both term and spot contracts.
"Currently we have two term contracts and each of those are limited to one year's duration," he said.
"One is with the Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation for about 400,000 tonnes and the balance with Amoco, an American company, also for Egyptian crude oil, for an amount of 1.5 million tonnes.
"The balance of the purchases that are made are spot purchases as and when the requirement might arise. The mixture of the two is very difficult to predict in advance."
Roberts said that SFF's cash income was 59 million rand in 1996, 198 million rand in 1997 and was projected to be 46 million rand this year.
"The way we view the market in the coming year is quite conservative and we anticipate a lower profit than we have had in the last two years," he said.
"Last year was an exceptional year but this is determined entirely by the movement in crude oil prices."

Roberts said SFF's focus this year would be on building relations with key players, examining opportunities in Africa, commercialising the tankfarms at Saldanha and Milnerton, marketing Soekor's crude oil and helping Mossgas with possible plans to supplement feedstocks.
